A_target.statement:
Let $R$ be a [[Definition:Dedekind Domain|Dedekind domain]].
The [[Definition:Ideal Class Group|ideal class group]] of $R$ is:
:$\map {\operatorname {Cl} } R = \map {\mathcal I} R / \map {\mathcal P} R$
and $\map {\operatorname {Cl} } R$ is [[Definition:Trivial Group|trivial]] {{iff}} $R$ is a [[Definition:Principal Ideal Domain|principal ideal domain]].

B_source.statement:
Let $A$ be an [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian group]] and $B$ a [[Definition:Subgroup|subgroup]].
Then the [[Definition:Quotient Group|quotient group]] $A / B$ is trivial {{iff}} $B = A$.

substitutions.the ambient abelian group: the group of nonzero fractional ideals under multiplication

derived.triviality of the quotient: every fractional ideal is principal, so the ring is a principal ideal domain
derived.the size of the quotient: the class number, measuring failure of unique factorization

object_map.reformulation: Measure failure of a property by collapsing the objects having it, so that triviality of the quotient is the property itself.

validity_conditions: The nonzero fractional ideals of a Dedekind domain form an abelian group under multiplication, which is what makes the quotient available.
The principal fractional ideals form a subgroup, since products and inverses of principal ideals are principal.
The Dedekind hypothesis is essential: in a general integral domain the fractional ideals need not be invertible and no group structure is present.
proof_plan: The non-zero [[Definition:Fractional Ideal|fractional ideals]] of $R$ form an [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian group]] $\map {\mathcal I} R$ under multiplication, as $R$ is a [[Definition:Dedekind Domain|Dedekind domain]].

The principal fractional ideals $\map {\mathcal P} R = \set {x R: x \in \map {\operatorname {Frac} } R^\times}$ form a [[Definition:Subgroup|subgroup]], as $x R \cdot y R = x y R$ and $\paren {x R}^{-1} = x^{-1} R$.

Form the [[Definition:Quotient Group|quotient]]:
:$\map {\operatorname {Cl} } R = \map {\mathcal I} R / \map {\mathcal P} R$

By the source result, $\map {\operatorname {Cl} } R$ is trivial {{iff}} every fractional ideal is principal.
This holds {{iff}} every ideal of $R$ is principal, that is, $R$ is a [[Definition:Principal Ideal Domain|PID]].
As a Dedekind domain is a [[Definition:Unique Factorization Domain|UFD]] {{iff}} it is a PID, $\map {\operatorname {Cl} } R$ measures the failure of unique factorization.
{{qed}}
